# ivue — Infinite Vue   [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/ivue.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/ivue) [![build status](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/infinite-system/ivue/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

**Plain classes. Full reactivity. One kilobyte.**

ivue builds Vue 3 reactivity out of plain TypeScript classes. Real
inheritance, real encapsulation, real polymorphism — on ordinary objects,
with nothing paid until first access. The whole engine is **1.1kb gzipped**
with zero dependencies.

```ts
import { Reactive } from 'ivue';
import { ref } from 'vue';

class $Counter {
  get count()  { return ref(0) }
  get double() { return this.count.value * 2 }  // plain getter — derives on read
  inc() { this.count.value++ }
}

export const Counter = Reactive($Counter);

const counter = new Counter();
counter.inc();
counter.count.value  // 1
counter.double       // 2, re-derived on read
```

## One idea, carried through

`Reactive()` transforms a class **once**. A getter returning `ref()` becomes
state: created on first touch, cached, stable forever. A plain getter stays
plain and re-derives on every read — reactive with zero allocation. Methods
bind themselves once, to the right `this`. Instances stay ordinary objects:
no proxy wraps them, no work happens at construction.

Inheritance, hot reload, teardown, speed — consequences of that one move.

## In a component

```vue
<script setup lang="ts">
import { Counter } from './Counter';

const counter = new Counter();

// the state destructure — every Ref the template touches, unwrapped uniformly
const { count } = counter;
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="counter.inc()">{{ count }} · double {{ counter.double }}</button>
</template>
```

The same class serves as a global store, a component ViewModel, or a domain
model. Composables plug straight in — the entire Vue ecosystem works inside
your classes:

```ts
import { useMouse } from '@vueuse/core';

class $Pointer {
  private get $mouse() { return useMouse() }  // created once, encapsulated
  get x() { return this.$mouse.x }
  get y() { return this.$mouse.y }
}
```

## The numbers

Measured, not promised — method and live in-browser benchmarks in
[the docs](https://infinite-system.github.io/ivue/).

| creating 100k instances | time | ivue is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ivue `new Class()`** | **0.7 ms** | the baseline |
| native `reactive()` | 36.7 ms | **55× faster** |
| composable factory | 42.8 ms | **64× faster** |

| heap per instance, same shape | heap | ivue is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ivue class, 60 getters** | **1.7 KB** | the baseline |
| composable, 60 closures | 12.8 KB | **7.7× lighter** |
| composable, 60 computeds | 31.1 KB | **18.6× lighter** |

Taken all the way down: a fully reactive spreadsheet model holding
**20,000,000 live cells at 4.7 bytes each** — 8.5× below the plain-object
floor — because in ivue, everything costs proportional to what's *observed*,
nothing costs proportional to what *exists*.

## Hard problems, solved together

Each of these sank earlier class-reactivity attempts. ivue ships all of them
as one coherent design:

- **Bound methods** — `this.method` is always correct, always the same reference.
- **Reactive inheritance** — deep `super.x.value` chains resolve level-safe.
- **Hot reload for classes** — behavior edits graft onto live instances, state intact.
- **Circular imports** — the namespace pattern resolves mutual references in any load order.
- **Writable getter types** — ref-returning getters type as writable; instances fully inferred.
- **Deterministic teardown** — `$watch` scopes per instance, `$stopEffects()` cleans up.
- **Memory** — derivations are shared prototype getters, not per-instance allocations.
- **Hot paths** — reads hoist to native ref speed with one line where it matters.

## Built for humans and AI

ivue ships with an [Operating Manual](https://infinite-system.github.io/ivue/guide/standard) —
the complete authoring standard as annotated templates, rules, and a review
checklist. It reads as documentation and works as a drop-in skill for AI
coding agents, so generated code follows the same standard your team writes.

## A note on the size

The v1 README said `1.1kb gzipped`. This engine — rewritten from scratch on a
different architecture: lazy prototype transform instead of per-instance
proxies, hot-reload grafting included — is **exactly 1.1kb gzipped** again.
Completely different, precisely the same weight.

> *Perfection is achieved, not when there is nothing more to add, but when
> there is nothing left to take away.* — Antoine de Saint-Exupéry

## Documentation

Full guide, principles, live benchmarks, and the API reference:
**https://infinite-system.github.io/ivue/**

6	# Getting Started
7	
8	## Install
9	
10	```sh
11	npm i ivue vue
12	```
13	
14	ivue has no runtime dependencies of its own; it works with any Vue 3.x.
15	
16	::: tip Hide `.value` while coding

18	[Vue plugin for VS Code / WebStorm](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=Vue.volar)
19	ecosystem includes inlay-hint and "hide `.value`" options that keep your source
20	clean.
21	:::
22	
23	## Your first reactive class
24	
25	Write a normal class. Declare state as getters returning `ref()`; derive with plain getters.
26	Wrap it with `Reactive()`.
27	
28	```ts
29	// counter.ts
30	import { Reactive } from 'ivue'
31	import { ref } from 'vue'
32	
33	class $Counter {
34	  get count() { return ref(0) }
35	  get double() { return this.count.value * 2 } // derived: plain getter
36	
37	  inc() { this.count.value++ }
38	  reset() { this.count.value = 0 }
39	}
40	
41	export const Counter = Reactive($Counter)
42	```
43	
44	Note what `double` is **not**: a `computed()`. Simple derivations stay plain
45	getters. They re-derive whenever a render reads them, cost zero bytes per
46	instance, and stay fully reactive. Reach for `computed()` only when the work
47	is expensive or you need render suppression. See
48	[Computed & Watch](/guide/computed-watch).
49	
50	The `$`-prefixed raw class (`$Counter`) is what children `extends`; the
51	transformed `Counter` is what you `new`. (More on this in
52	[Modules & Imports](/guide/modules) — for a single class you can skip the split
53	and just `Reactive(class Counter { … })`.)
54	
55	## Use it in a component
56	
57	```vue
58	<script setup lang="ts">
59	import { Counter } from './counter'
60	
61	const counter = new Counter()
62	
63	// destructure every Ref/Computed the template touches
64	const { count } = counter
65	</script>
66	
67	<template>
68	  <button @click="counter.inc">{{ count }} → {{ counter.double }}</button>
69	  <button @click="counter.reset">reset</button>
70	</template>
71	```
72	
73	That's it — `count` is the real ref, destructured straight off the instance (a state binding: unwrapped in the template, state at a glance); `counter.double` re-derives on every render; `counter.inc` is a stable
74	bound method. The component re-renders when `count` changes, exactly as if you'd
75	written refs by hand. Here is that exact class, running on this page:
76	
77	<DemoCounter />
78	
79	## What just happened
80	
81	- `new Counter()` created a **plain object** — no proxy.
82	- The first time you read `count`, its `ref(0)` was created and cached — the destructured binding IS that cached ref.
83	- `counter.double` is a plain getter — dotted in the template, because dotted means derivation. The render effect reads it, subscribes to `count` underneath, and re-derives on change. No allocation.
84	- `counter.inc` was bound to the instance once and reused.

PAT = re.compile(
    r'^(?P<indent>\s*)(?P<sig>(?:private |protected |readonly |static )?'
    r'(?:get |set )?[\w$#]+\((?P<params>[^()]*)\))\s*\{ (?P<body>.+?) \}(?P<trail>\s*(?://.*)?)$'
)

def expand_line(line):
    m = PAT.match(line)
    if not m:
        return None
    if 'class ' in line or '=>' in m.group('body') and m.group('body').count('{'):
        return None
    body = m.group('body')
    # skip bodies with unbalanced/nested braces (writable computed etc.)
    if body.count('{') != body.count('}'):
        return None
    indent = m.group('indent')
    trail = m.group('trail').strip()
    comment = f' {trail}' if trail else ''
    # split double statements on '; ' at top level (no parens tracking needed for our cases)
    parts = [body]
    if '; ' in body and '(' not in body.split('; ')[0]:
        parts = body.split('; ')
    lines = [f'{indent}{m.group("sig")} {{']
    for i, part in enumerate(parts):
        suffix = comment if i == len(parts) - 1 else ''
        lines.append(f'{indent}  {part}{suffix}')
    lines.append(f'{indent}}}')
    return lines

for path in FILES:
    p = pathlib.Path(path)
    src = p.read_text().split('\n')
    out, in_fence, changed = [], False, 0
    for line in src:
        if line.strip().startswith('```'):
            in_fence = not in_fence
            out.append(line)
            continue
        if in_fence:
            expanded = expand_line(line)
            if expanded:
                out.extend(expanded)
                changed += 1
                continue
        out.append(line)
    if changed:

- The `--` separates aws-vault's args from the command.
- A **plain `docker restart` of a container does NOT refresh credentials**
  (it keeps the old env). If S3 uploads fail with credential errors, do a
  full recreate — `aws-vault exec noone --duration 12h -- npm run restart`
  — not a container restart.
- **The agent shell is usually ALREADY inside an aws-vault subshell**
  (`AWS_VAULT=noone` set) — and its token may be long expired: check
  `$AWS_CREDENTIAL_EXPIRATION` against `date -u`. A nested
  `aws-vault exec` refuses to run ("running in an existing aws-vault
  subshell"). Mint a fresh session by unsetting the stale session vars

  env -u AWS_VAULT -u AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID -u AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY \

---
name: write-docs
description: Use when writing or editing any documentation in this repo — docs_v2 guide pages, README, invariants docs, sketch DESIGN/RESULTS files, or doc comments meant for readers. Encodes the house documentation style — timeless present tense with no edit-history residue, unpacked concepts over compressed jargon, ivue-standard code examples, and verified claims.
---

# write-docs — how documentation is written here

Documentation serves ONE person: the reader arriving fresh. Every rule below
derives from that. The reader was not present for our decisions, our earlier
drafts, or our corrections — and must never need to be.

## Timeless present — no edit-history residue

Docs describe what IS. They never narrate how the text got that way.

- **NEVER contrast against a phantom.** The failure mode: a first draft says
  X, it gets corrected to Y, and the rewrite says "it is Y, not X" or
  "previously X, but now Y". That X never shipped — it was a draft artifact.
  The reader has never seen X; referencing it introduces a concept that
  exists nowhere, purely to dismiss it. Write Y as if it were always Y.
- The test: **would this sentence make sense to someone who has read no
  earlier version of this document?** If a sentence exists only to close a
  door the reader never saw open, delete it.
- The exception is a REAL alternative a reader might actually bring with
  them (a Vue idiom, a rejected design that shipped elsewhere, a pattern
  from another library). Contrasting against those serves the reader —
  components.md's regime-history table earns its place because those
  regimes were genuinely tried and readers know them. Contrast earns its
  place by the reader's prior knowledge, never by our drafting history.
- Same discipline at the sentence level: no "actually", "instead we now",
  "it turns out", "as mentioned above we changed" — decision ceremony reads
  as churn and makes the reader re-litigate settled questions.

## Unpack concepts — density is not clarity

Write for a competent developer who does not share our head.

- **First use of a term of art gets its plain meaning in-line**: "a POJO — a
  plain JavaScript object with no proxy or class machinery", "detached
  scope — an effect scope no parent scope will ever stop". After the first
  unpacking, the short term is free to use.
- **No hard pivots.** A sentence that lurches between three compressed
  ideas with em-dash chains and untranslated jargon serves nobody. One idea
  per sentence; the technical term AND what it means; complete sentences
  over fragment chains (`A → B → fails` is a note to self, not prose).
- Terse is fine when the words are common; terse is hostile when the words
  are load-bearing jargon. When in doubt, spend the extra clause.
- **One concept, one name, everywhere.** If the docs call it an invariant,
  no page calls it a law, a rule, or a principle. A second name for the
  same thing reads as a second thing.
- **Never reference by number** ("see Principle #4", "rule 3 above") —
  numbering changes, and the reference forces the reader to go count.
  Reference by name and link to the anchor.

## Code in docs follows the ivue skill

Every code block is teaching code — someone WILL copy it.

- Apply the **ivue skill** to every example: proper multi-line member
  bodies (no `get x() { return ref(0) }` one-liners), domain-word
  identifiers (no `inst`, `qty`, `v`/`old` — `instance`, `quantity`,
  `newValue`/`oldValue`), thin closures delegating to methods, the
  namespace export with its three inline comments, the grouped state
  destructure in SFCs.
- **Example tiers**: a block with a filename comment (`// product.ts`) is a
  TEMPLATE — full canon, namespace pattern, everything. A block without a
  filename is a FRAGMENT — the minimum that proves the point, but still
  obeying every costless convention (naming, `.value`, multi-line form).
  Never write a "quick" example that models a banned pattern.
- SFC fragments are complete SFCs: `<script setup lang="ts">` present, a
  real `<template>` — never a floating template tag in a ts fence.
- If the docs demo a component live, the demo imports the SAME files the
  page shows — the page's code blocks are the demo's actual source.

## Claims are measured, verified, current

- Numbers carry their method and environment ("Measured on Vue 3.5, 20k
  instances, one full read pass"). "Measured, not promised" is the voice.
- Never state a behavior you haven't executed. Mount the component, run the
  snippet, build the site. A claim about reactivity semantics gets a test
  before it gets a sentence.
- After ANY docs change: `npm run build:docs` must pass, and anchors you
  link to must exist in the built HTML (VitePress won't fail on a dead
  in-page anchor).

## Repo mechanics (this codebase)

- **The skill is the source; standard.md is the mirror.** Edit
  `.claude/skills/ivue/SKILL.md`, then resplice `docs_v2/guide/standard.md`
  from the `# ivue (\`Reactive\`) — Operating Manual` marker and assert the
  bodies are byte-identical. Never edit the mirror directly.
- VitePress traps: literal `{{ }}` in prose SSR-compiles as interpolation
  (rephrase or v-pre); raw-HTML `href`/`src` are not base-prefixed (the
  markdown-it pass in config handles md files — Vue components use
  `withBase()`); frontmatter values starting with a backtick break YAML.
- Punchy one-line theses go in blockquotes — the theme styles every guide
  blockquote as an invariant card, so reserve `>` for statements that
  deserve it.
- Design changes are verified by screenshot (both themes) before claiming
  done; interactive demos by jsdom mount-and-drive.

## Self-review (run over your docs diff)

- [ ] No sentence references a draft state, a correction, or "the old way"
      that never shipped; everything reads timeless-present.
- [ ] Every term of art is unpacked at first use; no fragment-chain prose.
- [ ] One name per concept across all touched pages; no by-number references.
- [ ] Every code block passes the ivue skill checklist for its tier.
- [ ] Numbers have method + environment; behaviors were executed.
- [ ] Docs build passes; linked anchors exist in built HTML; skill mirror
      resynced if SKILL.md changed.

Read the embed — I can explain every anomaly you saw in production. Let me lay out my understanding before touching anything, since most of the task list hangs off the numbers story.

## The production embed bug — diagnosed

The DemoPerf benchmark is structurally broken as a measurement, and it's not a dev/prod semantics issue:

```ts
let sink: any;
v2ms.value = bench(() => {
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) sink = new V2();
});
```

Every iteration overwrites `sink`, so only the **last** instance ever escapes the loop. V8's escape analysis is entitled to elide the other 99,999 allocations — and in the production build, after minification and inlining, it does exactly that for `reactive(new Plain())` (0.0 ms) and mostly does it for the composable (0.1 ms). ivue's construction path is opaque enough that it *doesn't* get elided (1.5 ms) — so ivue is the only row paying for real allocations while the competitors report the cost of an optimized-away loop. We're benchmarking the JIT's dead-code elimination, not creation.

Second structural problem: the shapes aren't comparable. `$V2` has two ref-getters + a derived getter; `Plain` has two **plain number fields** (no reactivity per instance at all); the composable makes 2 refs + 1 eager computed. Three different amounts of work.

The fix for a real benchmark: identical member shape across all three, every instance stored into a pre-allocated array (`instances[i] = ...`), a post-pass that reads something from every instance so nothing is elidable, warmup passes, median of several runs. That harness fixes the embed *and* is what I'd use to re-test the static tables — at both 100k and 1M (agreed that 1M is the better headline; at ~7ms projected it's still a great number, and "10M in 50ms" already exists as the scaling line).

On your intuition that the composable should beat `reactive(new X())`: for *creation*, the reactive wrapper is genuinely cheaper — it allocates one proxy and defers everything, while the factory eagerly allocates 2 refs + 1 computed + closures. So 36.7 vs 42.8 is plausible, not obviously wrong — but I'll let the fixed harness settle it rather than argue from theory. If the honest numbers shrink the 55×/253× headlines, the headlines change; measured-not-promised cuts both ways.

## The template-boundary table — you're right, and here's the honest framing

"raw (the standard)" **is ivue** — reads on the raw ivue instance with no wrapper. The label should say so: something like **"ivue raw instance (the standard)"**.

And yes, the method row is the subtle one. `instance.method` is not raw-raw: every access goes through the engine's prototype getter → `toRaw` → symbol-cache lookup → return the cached bound function. That ~4.0 ns **is** ivue's indirection cost — a plain prototype method access is well under 1 ns. So the table isn't fabricated, but the column name "raw" implies zero machinery, which is the part that's a lie by labeling. Two fixes: rename the column, and add one honest sentence that the 4 ns *is* the engine's access indirection (the page's "Reads cost a little more" section already confesses the ~24 ns hot-loop figure, so this completes the story rather than contradicting it). I'll re-measure all nine cells with the fixed harness, and measure **access** and **call** separately for methods so we say precisely which one the number is.

Which sets up your method-hoisting suggestion perfectly — it's real and worth documenting: methods are referentially stable, so `const sortRows = this.sortRows` hoists the bound function once and the loop pays only the call, same shape as the ref hoist. I'll verify the speedup with the harness before writing it.

## The rest — my read, all agreed, no blockers

- **Homepage**: 4-line hero with "Performance by Design." as line three; the Zero-cost-creation feature card gets the "Performance by Design →" link; One-kilobyte card gets a punch line (my candidate: *"Stripped to the load-bearing core. An API you can hold in your head."*); "The numbers" → "Performance numbers"; **Start here above the numbers — yes, good idea** (visitors decide where to go; the receipts are there for those who scroll).
- **Nav**: new **Performance** section = The Reactive Model Layer, Performance by Design, Benchmarks; "At Scale" → **Advanced Patterns** (keeping Engine Under the Idiom + Flyweight there, with Model Layer moving out — confirm that's what you meant).
- **Model Layer rename**: it's really a benchmark-backed argument that models belong in reactivity. Candidates: **"Models at Scale: The Numbers"**, **"The Model Layer, Measured"**, or **"100,000 Live Entities"** (most concrete, most clickable). My pick: **"The Model Layer, Measured"** — says both what it is and that it's comparison material.
- **`inc()` → `increment()`** everywhere (hero, homepage, README, getting-started, demos) — clear ivue-skill naming violation I planted; will sweep with jsdom re-verification of the demos.
- **Baseline pills**: replace every `—` "ivue is" cell with the `the baseline` pill globally; the "embed measures production semantics" info box gets deleted (you're right — production disables HMR at build time, the box explains a dev-only artifact to production readers).
- **Hot loops formatting**: split the hoist line into two `const` statements and move both teaching comments onto their own lines above the code so nothing hides behind a horizontal scrollbar.

One question before I run: the re-bench happens on this Parallels VM, which is not the machine the original numbers came from — the new tables will say "Measured on Apple-silicon VM, Node 22 / Chromium" or whatever the environment turns out to be, and all headline multipliers get replaced wholesale with what actually measures. want your opinion, should it be standard.md or manual.md?

Keep **standard.md** — and I'd actually push the reasoning further than file naming:

**A manual describes; a standard governs.** Every library has a manual — it's the book you consult when confused. Almost no library ships a *standard* — a document that says "this is the one way we write this, humans and machines alike." That second thing is the genuinely novel artifact here, and it's the whole pitch of the page ("the same standard your team writes", the review checklist, the DO/NEVER table). Naming it `manual.md` would file it under reference material; `standard.md` names what makes it different.

**It matches the vocabulary the docs already use everywhere.** "The state-destructure standard", "the authoring standard", "raw + destructured state — the standard" in the components regime table, "the standard column" in the performance tables. One concept, one name — the page that defines the standard should be called the standard.

**The layering works as-is.** The page is "The Standard"; the document *inside* it is titled "Operating Manual" — that's not a contradiction, it's structure: the standard is the thing; the operating manual is its form (operational instructions an agent can execute). For the skill's own H1, "Operating Manual" is the right register — agents operate, they don't standardize.
